newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Russia said to sell strategic metals.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russia said to sell strategic metals.

text.p: Russia seems to be topping up hard currency earnings by selling metals again from its strategic stockpiles, traders reported on Tuesday.

Stocks became a source of exported metals during the collapse of the Soviet Union, when military demand for them declined, and in the early 1990s sales of aluminium were big eough to threaten a collapse of the world market.
The latest selling, if confirmed, would be on a smaller and less disruptive scale and involved some of the minor or so-called strategic metals - cobalt, mercury and titanium sponge.
Material had already moved to the minor metals market or was in the process of doing so, several European traders said.
They believed that 420 tonnes of cobalt, 30,000 76 lb flasks of mercury, 7,000 tonnes of titanium sponge and an undisclosed amount of chrome could be released from strategic stockpiles.
Earlier on Tuesday trade sources said that a large proportion of the cobalt had already been sold to a major trade organisation.
"It seems to be becoming a hard fact that the Russian government has given the go ahead for the release of the material," one London-based trader said.
But as usual in such matters the Russian authorities would not comment. Prices for the metals in question, after staying relatively stable, have started to show signs of cracking.
"Chrome and mercury have the potential to fall, while cobalt has eased but this is not entirely due to the talk of the sale," a trader said.
Despite the troubles in war-torn Zaire, a key supplier, cobalt prices have eased throughout most of the early part of 1997.
Russian cobalt was trading in a range of between $18 and $19 a lb according to some traders. Others said their range was lower at roughly between $17 and $18.

Uncertainties about Russian supply also affected the bigger market in base metals, particularly nickel, which on Monday had extended a strong rally on fears about labour unrest at the giant Norilsk metals complex in the Arctic.
But nickel, mainly used in making stainless steel, eased back on Tuesday below the key $8,000 per tonne threshold on the London Metal Exchange.
Traders said buying by speculative funds dried up and people baled out from a rally that had taken it up by 25 percent since the start of 1997.
Other base metals including aluminium and copper were also easier on Tuesday. Copper had made a new 8-1/2 month high at $2,385 per tonne on Monday before profit taking set in.
Gold was on hold awaiting Congressional testimony on the US economy on Wednesday by US Federal Reserve Board chairman Alan Greenspan.
Tuesday saw an afternoon London fix of $353.10, just five cents up from Monday.
Bellwether North Sea Brent crude oil futures stayed around their lowest in six months, below $20 a barrel, compared with around $25 late last year, on views that supply is ample.
Coffee, cocoa and sugar traded within ranges while US benchmark wheat futures eased, by some five cents on the Chicago Board of Trade March contract, to $3.70 per bushel.
Values were pressured by Sparks Companies analyst Brad Anderson who, in remarks prepared for USDA's annual Outlook Forum, projected U.S. wheat output at 2.44 billion bushels -
above a newly revised government outlook for 2.27 billion.
